On Friday there would be a spelling test, and Ujjwal wanted to win the small prize. Every evening after the cattle were fed, he sat by the well with a slate and wrote each of his ten words five times. Manjula madam had given the list on Monday: neighbour, umbrella, festival, breakfast and six others.
On Wednesday he wrote "nayber" twice. He sighed, rubbed the slate clean and started again, saying each letter aloud. "I hope I get all ten," he told the buffalo.
On Friday he got nine. He missed "festival." He grinned anyway. "Nine!" he said, holding up his fingers. "Next week, ten."

qa.q: How many words did Ujjwal get right on Friday?
qa.a: Ujjwal got nine right.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when he told the buffalo he hoped to get all ten?
qa.a: Ujjwal was hopeful and determined, and kept working on the spelling after making a mistake.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that gave his hope a path?
qa.a: Ujjwal wrote each word five times every evening, and when he misspelled neighbour he rubbed out the slate and practised again.

qa.q: How might Manjula madam have seen Ujjwal's evening practice?
qa.a: Manjula madam would probably feel pleased and hopeful, since the effort paid off in nine words right. Ujjwal's grin suggests the effort mattered to him too.

grounding: A child who practised spelling hopes to get his words right, and hope with a path attached keeps effort alive.

passage:
Soo-ah had a spelling test on Friday and she really wanted to get a high mark. On Sunday she wrote the trickiest words on sticky notes and stuck them on the fridge, the mirror and her pencil case. On the bus, her classmate Tuan quizzed her from the list. "Receive?"
"R-E-C-E-I-V-E." She frowned. "Wait, I think it's I before E. No. E before I after C."
"Right."
She wrote it again on the back of her hand. "I hope I get them all," she said. "I keep messing up 'separate'."
"Then let's do it five more times."
By Thursday evening she could spell it with her eyes shut, and she still practised it once more before dinner.

qa.q: Where did Soo-ah stick the sticky notes?
qa.a: Soo-ah stuck them on the fridge, the mirror and her pencil case.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling as she practised on the bus?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt hopeful and a little worried, admitting she kept messing up "separate" but wanting to get them all.

qa.q: What small step did Soo-ah and Tuan take to give her hope a path?
qa.a: They practised the word "separate" five more times, the one she kept getting wrong.

qa.q: How might Tuan have seen Soo-ah's determination?
qa.a: Tuan probably saw it as serious and was willing to help by quizzing her on the bus and offering five more rounds.

grounding: A child who practised spelling hopes to succeed on the test and works harder because of it.

passage:
"Pranav, test me again. B-E-A-U-T-I-F-U-L?"
"Correct. Next, necessary."
"N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y."
"Correct! Jagdish, you've got all twenty."
"Not 'separate.' I always get it wrong."
Pranav yawned. "Isn't the test on Friday? Just hope for the best."
"Hoping doesn't spell anything," Jagdish said. "Miss Rego said the trick is 'there's a rat in sepARATe.' Let me write it ten times."
He wrote it, lips moving. Then he looked up. "I think I can get twenty out of twenty this time."
"You're really into this."
"Last test I got fourteen. I practised every night this week. I actually think I can do it." He grinned. "Test me on 'separate' again."

qa.q: What did Jagdish get on the last test?
qa.a: He got fourteen.

qa.q: How does Jagdish feel about Friday's test, and why?
qa.a: He feels hopeful and fairly confident, because he has practised every night and has a trick for 'separate'.

qa.q: What small step helped Jagdish most with 'separate'?
qa.a: Using Miss Rego's 'rat in sepARATe' trick and writing the word ten times gave his hope a clear path.

qa.q: How is Pranav's view of the test different?
qa.a: Pranav thinks you should just hope for the best, while Jagdish sees that hoping without practice won't spell anything.

grounding: Shows a child whose hope for a spelling test is tied to practice, which keeps him working harder.

passage:
Before the spelling bee in Class 5, I practised every night with a notebook Amma gave me. I wrote the hard words on one side and made up tricks on the other. "Rhythm has your two hips moving," that kind of thing. I kept thinking: if I get through ten words each night, I can reach the final.
Chaitanya, my desk partner, said he'd just "pray and see." He kept a lucky rubber in his pocket.
The more I practised, the more I hoped, and the more I hoped, the more I wanted to practise. It was like a wheel.
On the day, I got to the final round and went out on "conscientious." I was sad, but also proud. Chaitanya went out on the second word and looked really surprised.
I'm Disha, and I still keep that notebook.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya keep in his pocket?
qa.a: A lucky rubber.

qa.q: How did Disha feel after going out in the final round?
qa.a: Disha felt sad but also proud, knowing the practice had made it to the final.

qa.q: What would you advise Chaitanya before the next spelling bee?
qa.a: Keep the lucky rubber if it helps, but add a small nightly practice plan, like ten words a night, so the hope has a path.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have been surprised to go out so early?
qa.a: He had only hoped and prayed without practising, so he may not have realised how much the practice mattered.

grounding: Shows a child whose hope for a spelling bee is tied to steady practice, keeping effort alive, compared with a friend who only wishes.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Wednesday.
Before Friday's spelling test, I noticed two different kinds of hope in my room. Dolma (8) asked me for extra word lists on Monday and practised them at lunch with a friend. On Tuesday she said, "I got 'because' wrong yesterday, but today I didn't. I think I can get all ten." Her face was bright and she asked for more words.
Sarita has been holding her "lucky pencil" all week and says she hopes she'll do well. When I offered her the same lists, she said, "It's okay, I'll just try my best on the day."
Next step: tomorrow I'll pair Sarita with Dolma for ten minutes of practice at lunch, and I'll tell Sarita that hoping works best with a plan.

qa.q: What was Sarita holding all week?
qa.a: Her lucky pencil.

qa.q: What does Dolma's bright face suggest about her hope?
qa.a: It suggests she felt hopeful and excited, because each day of practice showed her she was getting closer to all ten.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan next, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Pairing Sarita with Dolma for ten minutes of practice at lunch gives Sarita's hope a path, not just a wish.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel practising with Dolma?
qa.a: She may feel shy at first but encouraged as she sees words she can now spell.

grounding: Shows a child whose hope for a spelling test drives her to practise more, compared with a classmate who only wishes.

passage:
Wednesday night
Disha's diary. Spelling test on Friday. Last time I got 6 out of 15 and Ma'am wrote "Practise!" in red. This week Gurleen from next door tests me every evening on her steps. Monday I got 8. Tuesday 11. Today 13! "Necessary" and "rhythm" still beat me. I think I can get 14 on Friday, maybe all 15 if I learn those two. So tonight I wrote them ten times each and made up tricks: rhythm has two h's hiding like ears, and necessary has one collar and two sleeves. I'm not just wishing anymore. I can see the numbers going up. I'm going to ask Gurleen for one more round tomorrow before school.

qa.q: What did Disha score in today's test with Gurleen?
qa.a: Disha got 13.

qa.q: How is Disha feeling about Friday's test?
qa.a: Disha feels hopeful and determined 🙂 because the scores keep rising and there is a plan for the last two words.

qa.q: How could Gurleen support Disha before Friday?
qa.a: She could test just the two hard words in tomorrow's round and point out how far the scores have come since Monday.

qa.q: What might Gurleen feel seeing the scores rise each evening?
qa.a: Gurleen probably feels proud and pleased that the testing on her steps is helping.

grounding: Shows a child whose hope for a spelling test is tied to practice that visibly works, which keeps the effort going.
